title: elastic-burst-scheduling-and-isolation-prd-draft
content:
Summary:

This PRD proposes Elastic Burst Scheduling (EBS) for Redwood Dedicated: a tenant-aware, credit-based short-term burst system combined with lane-based isolation and smarter autoscaling policies. The goal is to let customers exceed reserved baseline throughput temporarily while preserving hard isolation guarantees for tenants that require strict performance or regulatory isolation.

Problem statement:

Customers purchase reserved GPU pools to guarantee throughput and latency for production workloads. Two common pain points: 1) burst capacity is either unavailable or too coarse (manual increases, long lead times), and 2) attempts to share spare capacity across tenants cause noisy-neighbor incidents or unpredictable latency spikes. Current Dedicated model lacks a nimble, observable, and policy-driven mechanism to let some customers safely burst while preserving isolation for others.

Goals:
- Allow short-duration bursts beyond reserved baseline (minutes to hours) with predictable cost/limits.
- Maintain hard isolation lanes where tenants can opt-in to strict non-preemption and bounded latency SLOs.
- Provide fair, auditable burst accounting (credits, throttles, chargebacks).
- Integrate with existing autoscaling to reduce manual ops and avoid oscillations.
- Expose clear console UX and API for configuring burst envelopes, priorities, and fallback behaviors.

Non-goals (out of scope):
- Implementing new hardware-level preemption primitives (we assume current GPU scheduling capabilities).
- Building peer-to-peer cross-customer sharing incentives or marketplace.

High-level design:

1) Burst Credits and Envelopes
- Each dedicated contract has a Reserved Baseline capacity (RB) and an Elastic Burst budget (EB) measured in GPU-minutes or token-equivalent throughput. EB accumulates at a configurable rate (e.g., 10% of RB per day) up to a maximum cap (e.g., 24h of RB).
- When traffic spikes, the tenant can consume EB to run above RB for short periods; consumption is strictly metered and reflected in billing.
- Console shows current EB balance, accrual rate, and historical usage.

2) Isolation Lanes
- We introduce 3 isolation lanes per pool: Strict, Flexible, and Shared.
  - Strict: no preemption, no noisy neighbor sharing; ideal for regulated/latency-sensitive tenants (higher price).
  - Flexible: allowed to burst using EB but may be preempted by Strict lane under extreme cluster contention (preemption policy is explicit and auditable).
  - Shared: behavour similar to current best-effort nodes; can use leftover capacity after RB+EB but with lowest priority.
- Tenants pick default lane at purchase and can request lane changes via support or API with guardrails.

3) Autoscaler integration
- Autoscaler continues to manage long-term capacity (scale-up/scale-down based on sustained load). EBS hooks into autoscaler as a short-term buffer layer:
  - If global cluster free capacity > threshold, autoscaler will avoid immediate scale-ups and allow bursts to consume excess until EB is depleted or certain time limit is hit.
  - If multiple tenants simultaneously consume EB and cluster headroom falls below safety margin, autoscaler will evaluate either pursuing additional Reserved-scale actions (when commitment or policy allows) or invoking preemption rules depending on lanes.
- Autoscaler needs smoothing windows and minimum up/down cooldowns to avoid thrash from burst events.

4) Preemption & Fairness rules
- Preemption is lane-aware and uses a priority score: Strict > (Flexible by EB balance & SLA tier) > Shared.
- Preemption decisions must be explainable and logged for 30 days (which tenant was preempted, why, fallback taken).
- Preemption granularity: request-level (abort queued jobs), connection draining (for in-flight streams) with configurable drain time (default 10s), or model-variant fallback to lower-capacity runtime (e.g., quantized instance).

5) Cost & Billing
- EB consumption is billed at a premium rate relative to baseline per-minute cost. Billing shows line-items: RB consumption, EB consumption, overtime charges.
- Alerts and soft-limits: tenants can set notification thresholds for EB usage to avoid surprise bills.

APIs / Config model:
- New fields on Dedicated pool config (examples):
  - burst_envelope: {accum_rate_per_day: "float", max_accrual_minutes: "int", enabled: "bool"}
  - isolation_lane: "strict|flexible|shared"
  - burst_priority: "numeric" (used within flexible lane for tie-breaking)
  - preempt_behavior: "drain|abort|fallback-variant"
Note: above would be represented as JSON in the API; console will show simple toggles/inputs.

Telemetry & SLOs:
- New metrics to capture:
  - eb_balance_minutes (per-tenant)
  - eb_consumption_rate (1m/5m/1h)
  - preemption_events (count + reason)
  - lane_violations (attempts to exceed allowed burst without EB)
  - perceived_p99_latency_change_during_burst
- Success criteria (30/60/90 days):
  - <5% of Dedicated tenants report perceived latency regressions attributable to neighbor bursts.
  - EB billing disputes <1% of burst events.
  - Autoscaler avoids unnecessary scale-ups in >60% of short spike cases where EB can cover load.

Console UX and operator controls:
- Pool overview: RB, EB balance, recent burst events, lane composition.
- Controls: toggle EB enable, set accrual rate, set max cap, set default lane.
- Incident playback: timeline view showing when EB was consumed, autoscaler decisions, and preemption actions with links to logs/traces.

Operational considerations:
- Safety guard: a global cluster safety knob that can disable EB consumption when we detect systemic capacity pressure (manual + automated thresholds).
- Audit trail: every burst consumption and preemption must be logged to an immutable audit store (for compliance customers).
- Testing: staged rollout with canary tenants; simulate high-burst scenarios in test clusters and verify autoscaler/eviction behavior.

Rollout plan (high level):
1) Design + proto (Q4): implement EB accounting in control plane, basic console surfaces, simulate in test clusters.
2) Internal beta (Q1): enable on 10% of Dedicated pools for low-risk tenants. Collect telemetry.
3) External beta (Q2): invite select customers with support follow-up and billing opt-in.
4) GA (Q3): full product with pricing and support docs.

Open questions / decisions required:
- Should EB accrual be shared at org-level or per-pool? (org-level allows cross-pool smoothing but complicates chargeback)
- Maximum safe preemption drain time for streaming workloads vs inference latency budgets?
- Pricing: what premium should EB consumption bear relative to baseline to balance signal vs adoption?
- Regulatory: Strict lane needs SLA language and potential legal addendum for compliance buyers.

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Misconfigured accrual rates cause large, unexpected bills. Mitigation: default conservative accrual, guardrails, and opt-in for billing.
- Risk: Autoscaler thrash when many tenants burst. Mitigation: global smoothing windows, cap on concurrent EB consumption per region.
- Risk: Customers misinterpret lane guarantees. Mitigation: clear console labeling, docs, and contractual language.

Appendix: sample tenant flow
- Tenant A has RB=100 GPU-minutes/hr, EB accrual 10%/day, cap=24h. Unexpected marketing event causes 6x traffic for 3 hours. EB covers 3 hours of extra capacity; tenant sees EB balance drop, billing reflect premium EB usage, and no preemption occurs because lane was Flexible and cluster had headroom.

- Tenant B in Shared lane tries to burst at same time: they get best-effort capacity until Shared's limit is reached, then are preempted in favor of Flexible/Strict lanes. Logs show preemption reason and time.

Next steps:
- Align with infra on preemption primitives and autoscaler hooks.
- Prototype EB accounting in control plane and an API shim.
- Draft pricing experiments and legal language for Strict lane.

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus review on the lane definitions and preemption semantics — these are the most likely to change during engineering feasibility discussions.
- Call out any missing telemetry or console surfaces you'd find essential for customer trust.
